summary: Runs 1 (BrickWork Pro) and 3 (SP Sixty Driving) read as credible sets of accounts for the trades described. Run 2 (Precision Code) is not credible: its Income Tax sheet applies the higher rate from £37,701 of taxable income with no additional-rate band, so a £226,508 profit is taxed as if the 40% band ran indefinitely, and the P&L presents the full £78,035 income tax as "Tax at basic rate".

concerns.figure: Tax at Higher Rate 70,494.8 / Total Income Tax 78,035
concerns.where: Run bst-scenario-basic, Income Tax sheet cells E9/E10 and P&L C32
concerns.why: Taxable income of £213,938 is split at £37,701 into basic and higher rate only. A sole trader with £226,508 taxable profit crosses the £100,000 personal allowance taper (the £12,570 allowance should be fully abated) and the £125,140 additional-rate threshold (45%). The sheet shows the full personal allowance and no additional-rate band, so income tax is materially understated for a profit of this scale. This is a substantive misstatement of the headline tax figure, not a rounding or presentation point.

concerns.figure: Tax at basic rate 78,035 (P&L C32) while Income Tax line C30 shows 0
concerns.why: The whole income tax charge, including £70,494.80 taxed at 40%, is labelled "Tax at basic rate" on the face of the P&L, and the "Income Tax" line immediately above it reads 0. A reader of the accounts would take the basic-rate label at face value. The same presentation appears in the other two runs, but there it is harmless because all tax genuinely falls in the basic band.

concerns.figure: New Asset Cost (Plant & Machinery) 1,800 against Total Original Cost 39,000
concerns.where: Run bst-scenario-basic, Fixed Assets sheet E67 vs E1
concerns.why: The reported single addition of £1,800 is only the first of three additions; the schedule total of £39,000 agrees to the journal, so this reconciles, but the £1,800 figure on its own is easy to misread as the whole year's capital spend. Worth a look at how the report picks the addition row.

concerns.figure: Employee Costs 0 with sub-contract labour of 20,000 in Direct Costs
concerns.where: Run bst-brickwork-pro-nonvat, Profit & Loss Account C11 and C7
concerns.why: Not an error — the scenario states sub-contract labour is bought in as a direct cost and there is no payroll, so a nil employee cost line is the product working as designed and the £20,000 direct cost is the labour. Recorded only so a reader is not surprised by a builder with no wages.

concerns.where: Run bst-sp-sixty, Profit & Loss Account C15
concerns.why: Fuel, insurance and repairs of £2,708 plus £580 repairs is on the low side for a full-time private hire driver turning over £38,000 on actual-cost basis (no mileage claim is in play). It is within the range of a driver on a leased or licensed-operator arrangement where costs sit in Other Expenses (£1,580), so it does not block the run, but it is the figure to check first.

concerns.figure: Capital allowance 200 with no motor vehicle in the fixed asset schedule
concerns.where: Run bst-sp-sixty, Fixed Assets E1 and Purchase Analysis
concerns.why: A taxi business with only £200 of capital additions and no vehicle on the schedule implies the car is not owned by the trade. Consistent with the scenario as written (one addition of £200), so not a fail, but a reader would expect to see how the vehicle is held.
